A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MetaUrban and MetaUrban-12K. Their complete text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the revised title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original PointNav and SocialNav benchmark results, generalization and density ablations, object-distribution analyses, and simulator-speed measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds mechanical-design evaluations, terrain-traversal experiments, urban-specific validation analyses, and PPO seed-variability results.

M1.justification: v1 states that terrain maps can serve as substrates. v2 Section 3.1 introduces a procedural terrain generator that connects five types of primitives using Wave Function Collapse and assigns materials with different friction coefficients. This substantially extends scene generation; the existing object-retrieval and crowd-population procedures largely remain.

E1.justification: MetaUrban-12K and the two navigation tasks are retained. v2 adds progressively difficult slope, stair, and rough-terrain traversal scenarios, pedestrian-distribution scenarios, and an indoor-versus-urban object-distribution analysis using ProcTHOR. Appendix I also reports preliminary real-world Go2 and COCO trials, although their evaluation is only qualitative.

E2.justification: The seven navigation baselines in Table 1 remain PPO, PPO-Lag, PPO-ET, IQL, TD3+BC, BC, and GAIL. ProcTHOR, already present in v1's background and simulator-feature comparison, becomes an empirical object-distribution comparator in v2 Appendix E and Figure 26.

E3.justification: The established navigation benchmark settings are retained. New protocols vary mechanical specifications during PPO training, apply a fixed forward policy on increasingly difficult terrains with displacement and time-to-fall metrics, compare 10 m versus 410 m training horizons, and vary pedestrian density and spatial placement (Section 4.2 and Appendices D.3 and E).

E4.justification: Beyond the retained generalization, scaling, and density ablations, v2 investigates sensitivity to speed and steering limits, wheel geometry and terrain, training horizons, and pedestrian distributions. Appendix E also analyzes urban-versus-indoor object composition. These additions test substantial new questions about mechanical constraints and the need for urban-specific simulation.

E5.justification: Appendix H newly reports PPO training with different seeds and success rates of 0.695 ± 0.014 on MetaUrban-test and 0.638 ± 0.060 on MetaUrban-unseen. Neither the seed count nor the meaning of ± is specified. The existing ten-run FPS measurements with standard errors are unchanged.

E6.justification: All Table 1 values and the original ablation plots remain unchanged. v2 adds mechanical-variant results (Table 2), terrain-traversal results (Table 9), horizon and pedestrian results (Table 10), object-distribution comparisons, seed summaries, and qualitative real-world transfer findings. For example, Table 10 reports 10% versus 41% success under short- versus long-horizon training; these are newly reported conditions, not version-to-version performance gains.

T1.justification: The layout-sampling definitions in Appendix B.1 and the PPO-Lag and reward equations (1)–(2) are retained. v2 introduces no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations; its terrain metrics and mechanical explanations are empirical.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction reposition MetaUrban around AI-driven urban micromobility and make the influence of mechanical structures on policy learning and execution a central contribution absent from v1. The novelty claim becomes explicitly about the first simulator for this domain. The original compositional-generation, generalization, and safety claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting mechanical design to mobility, safety, and terrain stability, and interprets its new controls as validating urban-specific simulation requirements. Appendix I adds an explicit sim-to-real discussion, qualitative transfer claims involving abstract observations and domain randomization, and planned realism improvements. Most earlier limitations remain, while robot-specific tasks are reframed as additional capability learning.

D1.justification: v2 adds terrain-construction details and numerical speed, steering, force, friction, and wheel-dimension specifications for the new experiments. Existing benchmark hyperparameters, hardware, training times, and planned code/data access remain substantially unchanged. The datasheet changes the reported collection date from May to September 2024 without explaining whether existing data were replaced.

R1.justification: The research positioning shifts from urban embodied AI and sociology toward micromobility and mechanical-design evaluation. v2 adds micromobility literature and terrain/navigation references such as Gumin and Lee et al., removes some sociology/planning references, and strengthens its distinctions from social-navigation simulators. The existing simulator survey and feature-comparison membership are largely retained.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten around micromobility. Object/Assets Retrieval becomes Obstacle Retrieval, and main-text zero-shot terminology becomes unseen evaluation. The standalone dataset section moves into Appendix C, experimental exposition is reorganized, and several appendix sections and an overview are added.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening illustration with a platform overview and a separate motivation figure, removes v1 Figure 4's object-placement examples, and relocates dataset statistics from Figure 6 to Appendix Figure 25. It adds Tables 2, 9, and 10 and Figure 26, reduces and wraps text around the ground-plan diagram, and reformats headers and tables. The original ablation graphics are retained.

improvement.justification: The new mechanical-design, terrain, and urban-specific control experiments make the simulator's capabilities more assessable than v1's delivery-bot benchmarks alone. These gains are qualified by incomplete statistical reporting and overextended interpretations: Appendix H omits seed counts and uncertainty definitions, while Table 2 shows intersection cost rising from 1.50 to 1.64 for the slower COCO variant despite the text claiming improved safety. The additions provide useful validation, but their reporting limits the overall quality gain.
